sections.h2: What should a Garfield Heights seller know first?
sections.html:
Garfield Heights requires a point-of-sale inspection before a house changes hands, and that rule shapes every sale in the city. A seller has to obtain a Certificate of Inspection from the Building Department, and the buyer cannot take title without a Compliance Certificate.

The city sits in Cuyahoga County on the southeast side of Cleveland, covers about 7.23 square miles of land, and has ZIP codes 44105, 44125 and 44128. It began as the Village of South Newburgh in 1907, became Garfield Heights Village in 1919, and was incorporated as a city in 1930 when the population hit 5,000. The name comes from Garfield Park. Wikipedia lists a mayor and seven wards under a charter that took effect in 1956.

The sections below walk through the inspection, the county transfer steps and the neighborhood facts that matter when you price.

sections.h2: How does the Garfield Heights point-of-sale inspection work?
sections.html:
Under Chapter 1313 of the city's codified ordinances, the owner must have a Certificate of Inspection before selling, transferring or agreeing to sell, and must show the buyer either that certificate or a Certificate of Compliance issued within a year before the agreement.

The city's inspection page and the ordinance set out the steps:

  • The owner or an agent applies on the Building Commissioner's form, and the inspection happens within ten days after the application and fee are received.
  • The certificate follows within ten working days after the inspector gains access and lists code violations found, which the owner must correct within 90 days unless the commissioner extends the time for good cause.
  • The fee is $200 for a dwelling and $300 for a commercial building. Each re-inspection after the first two costs $35, and a missed appointment without one business day of notice costs $25.
  • The buyer signs an acknowledgment of receiving the certificate, and a copy goes to the Building Department as a condition of transferring title.
  • If violations remain at closing, escrow of at least $100 and equal to 110 percent of the higher of two written repair estimates is required, or an approved bond.

The ordinance does not apply to a transfer by inheritance or gift where no real sale is intended. Escrow agents may not transfer title or release funds until the chapter has been satisfied, so start the application before you accept an offer.

sections.h2: What documents does a Garfield Heights buyer have to sign?
sections.html:
The city's page lists a notarized Buyer's Acknowledgement Form, which has to be returned in original to the office. A business buyer must designate an agent, and an out-of-state business must register with the Ohio Secretary of State as a foreign corporation before the Compliance Certificate is issued.

If the buyer is assuming outstanding violations, a notarized Affidavit is also needed, and the buyer has 90 days from the transfer date to finish the repairs. The seller's signature on the affidavit is not required for bank-owned, Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac properties. The page offers separate forms for individuals and businesses, a consent form for an interior inspection, and a snow-covered-property agreement.

The Building and Housing office is at 5407 Turney Road, 2nd floor, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 3:45 p.m., and accepts applications by email at buildingdept@garfieldhts.org or by fax. The city says emails are processed within two business days, and fees increased in 2025.

sections.h2: How do Cuyahoga County recording and transfer work for a Garfield Heights sale?
sections.html:
Cuyahoga County combines the old auditor, recorder and engineer functions in the Fiscal Office's Transfer and Recording division at 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, Cleveland. Every transfer needs either a DTE 100 statement of value or a DTE 100-EX exemption form.

The division's page lists the standard recording fee as $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each additional page, effective October 24, 2024 under Senate Bill 94. Office hours are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and recording hours end at 4:00 p.m. The phone number is 216-443-2060. Ask the Fiscal Office for the conveyance fee that applies to your sale.

Deed preparation counts as the practice of law in Ohio, according to the division, and county staff cannot give legal advice. A seller may prepare their own deed, and it must follow the Ohio Revised Code. ORC 5301.01 requires the signature to be acknowledged before an officer such as a notary.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers show for Garfield Heights?
sections.html:
Garfield Heights is one of the more affordable inner-ring Cleveland suburbs, which makes it attractive to investors and first-time owners. The median owned home is valued under $110,000, and the city lost population over the past five years.

sections.h2: What do buyers see around Garfield Heights?
sections.html:
The city has a mix of Polish, Slovene, German, Italian and Irish heritage alongside a growing share of African American residents. Streets are dense: about 4,119 residents per square mile in 2020.

Parks and amenities that buyers ask about include the Dan Kostel Recreation Center on Turney Road, with an outdoor summer pool and an indoor ice rink, and the Garfield Park Reservation, part of Cleveland Metroparks, in the northeast corner on the Cleveland border. The Wargo Farms parcel, about 45 acres, was sold to Cleveland Metroparks in 2023 for green space and trails.

The Garfield Heights school system runs three elementary schools, one middle school and Garfield Heights High School under a five-member elected board. Catholic options in the city include St. Benedict and Trinity High School. For jobs, the Highland Park development, once City View Center and built on a former landfill, was bought out of receivership in 2020 and has added companies such as MPAC Switchback, MTech, Innoplast and Thermoprene.

sections.h2: What are the options for selling a Garfield Heights house fast?
sections.html:
Because of the inspection rule, speed depends on who handles the violations.

  • Agent listing: the buyer sees the certificate up front, and you fix cited items inside 90 days or fund the escrow.
  • Sale as-is to an investor: the buyer can assume violations through the affidavit and finish repairs within 90 days of transfer.
  • Inherited property: a transfer by inheritance or gift without a bona fide sale falls outside the point-of-sale chapter.

The Building Department also tracks a Cuyahoga County demolition list for homes in the city. A house with several violations and unpaid liens may be better sold than repaired.

faqs.q: Do I need an inspection to sell a house in Garfield Heights?
faqs.a: Yes for a sale. Chapter 1313 requires a Certificate of Inspection before you sell or agree to sell, and the buyer needs a Compliance Certificate to take title. The $200 dwelling fee applies.

faqs.q: How long do I have to fix violations from the inspection?
faqs.a: The owner has 90 days from the certificate to correct cited items, unless the Building Commissioner extends it for good cause. A buyer assuming violations also has 90 days after transfer, under the affidavit.

faqs.q: What if I can't afford repairs before closing?
faqs.a: Violations left open at closing require escrow of at least $100 and 110 percent of the higher of two written estimates, or an approved bond. Selling as-is to a buyer who signs the affidavit is another route.

faqs.q: Where do I record a Garfield Heights deed?
faqs.a: Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office, Transfer and Recording, 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, Cleveland. Filing a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX comes with the deed, and standard recording costs $39 for two pages.

faqs.q: Is an inherited Garfield Heights house exempt from the point-of-sale rule?
faqs.a: The ordinance does not apply to transfers by inheritance or gift where no bona fide sale is intended. A true sale of the inherited house is covered, so ask the Building Department before listing.
